title: Council Post: The Rise Of Artificial Intelligence In Finance
text:
Chris Kinyua is the Founding Engineering Lead at Fizz—a movement to give the next generation a brighter financial future.
In an era marked by rapid technological advancements, artificial intelligence (AI) stands at the forefront of innovations transforming industries across the globe. However, AI's integration into financial institutions is not just a trend; it represents a fundamental shift in how these entities operate. Financial institutions, traditionally rooted in conventional practices, are embracing AI to drive product innovation and ensure they remain competitive and relevant for future generations. The adoption of AI is driven by the need for greater efficiency, better customer experience and robust security measures in the industry. This article explores how AI is revolutionizing financial institutions, the benefits it brings and the challenges that must be navigated.
Enhancing The Customer’s Experience
One of the most visible impacts of AI in financial services is the transformation of customer experience. Chatbots and virtual assistants, powered by large language models, provide customers with 24/7 support, addressing queries and solving problems in real time. AI-powered chatbots are capable of handling a wide range of customer interactions, from answering simple questions about account balances to providing detailed information about complex financial products. This level of service availability ensures that customers receive timely assistance, improving their overall experience and fostering loyalty. Additionally, AI-driven tools can handle multiple interactions simultaneously, significantly increasing efficiency compared to human-operated customer service centers.
Personalized banking experiences are another significant benefit. AI algorithms analyze vast amounts of customer data to offer tailored financial advice, product recommendations and investment strategies. For example, AI can help identify spending patterns, suggest budgeting tips or recommend investment opportunities that align with a customer’s financial goals and risk tolerance. This level of personalization was previously unattainable at scale, but AI makes it possible. With such personalization and support, customers are more empowered than ever to reach their financial goals.
Strengthening Security And Fraud Detection
Security is a huge concern for today’s financial institutions. With the advent of digital banking and e-commerce, fraud has grown to gargantuan levels. Without automation and intelligent tools, it is much more difficult to defend against online fraud in the modern era. Many financial institutions are thus leveraging AI for fraud detection and prevention through sophisticated machine algorithms that identify unusual patterns in customer behavior. These models continuously learn from the massive datasets generated by users, improving their ability to flag fraudulent activities with high accuracy in a way that humans could never achieve at scale.
AI systems like these can flag suspicious transactions and interactions in real time, allowing an institution to act swiftly and prevent potential losses. In addition to real-time fraud detection, AI can also often predict and mitigate risks before they happen. This proactive approach helps enable financial institutions to strengthen their defenses and reduce the likelihood of fraud. This not only helps protect the financial institution but also builds customer confidence in the safety of their financial assets.
Data-Driven Decision Making
Historically, the financial sector has relied heavily on human expertise for decision-making processes. However, the sheer volume of data generated in today’s digital age requires more advanced analytical tools. AI, with its ability to process and analyze massive datasets at incredible speeds, provides a solution that is both efficient and highly accurate. By leveraging AI, financial institutions can uncover valuable insights from their data, enabling them to forecast market trends, customer behaviors and potential risks with unprecedented accuracy.
Streamlining Operations
Many back-office functions in a financial institution, such as data entry, reconciliation, generating reports, data backups, etc., can be automated by AI. Automation of these mundane and repetitive tasks not only enhances efficiency but also reduces the likelihood of human error. This frees up employees to focus on product development and strategic activities. Financial institutions that effectively use automation may also be able to operate with leaner teams, reducing overhead expenses. This can generate considerable savings that can be reinvested into innovation and customer-centric initiatives.
Challenges And Considerations
While the benefits of AI in financial services are substantial, there are challenges that institutions must address. Data privacy and security concerns are paramount. As AI systems handle sensitive financial information, robust measures must be in place to protect this data from breaches and misuse.
In addition, AI can be subject to bias. Many financial datasets used for training AI may have some inherent bias within them. AI systems trained on these datasets will unknowingly propagate these biases and reinforce them if not corrected early enough. Financial institutions must build monitoring and mitigation tools around their AI systems to help ensure the outcomes they provide are fair and that no segments of their customer base are disadvantaged.
Moreover, effective integration of AI requires significant investment in technology infrastructure and talent. Financial institutions must ensure their teams have the skills and knowledge to implement and manage AI solutions effectively. This may involve retraining existing staff and hiring new talent with specialized expertise. The initial investment can be substantial, but the long-term benefits of AI integration make it a worthwhile endeavor.
Regulatory compliance is another critical consideration. Financial institutions must navigate complex regulatory landscapes to ensure their AI applications adhere to legal and ethical standards. Collaboration with regulators can help in establishing guidelines that foster innovation while protecting consumers. It is essential for financial institutions to maintain transparency and accountability in their use of AI to build trust with both regulators and customers.
Conclusion
The journey of AI in transforming financial institutions is just beginning. As technology continues to evolve, we can expect even more profound changes in the coming years. AI will become increasingly integrated into every aspect of financial services. Looking ahead, the institutions that embrace AI will be better positioned to meet the demands of consumers. However, navigating the challenges of integration, data privacy and regulatory compliance is crucial for successful implementation. The financial institutions that do this correctly will lead the way, setting new standards for excellence and innovation in the industry.

title: Why Apple Stock Is A Safe Haven In An Uncertain Market
text:
The markets are having a tough couple of weeks, with the S&P 500 declining by about 7% over the past month, while the Nasdaq-100 has declined by 12.5%. Even Apple stock, which is viewed as a safe haven of sorts, hasn’t really been immune to the sell-off, declining by about 8% over the last month. The recent sell-off comes amid concerns about a recession in the U.S. after a tough jobs report for July. Moreover, consumers have also been feeling the pinch of high interest rates and inflation with pandemic-era savings dwindling. However, we think Apple stock could hold up better than the broader market if there is an economic downturn.
Strong Financial Performance And Position
Apple’s revenues are expected to scale to record highs this year, with sales projected to grow 9% to $390.27 billion, per consensus estimates, led by growth in emerging markets such as India. Apple has also been astute at managing its costs. Apple also grew its gross margins to 46% for the first nine months of this fiscal year, reaching near all-time highs, up from about 44% in the year-ago period, driven by a more favorable product mix, and higher service sales. Investors treated Apple stock as a safe haven of sorts through the Covid-19 era with its stock price and price to earnings multiple expanding to multi-year highs. This trend could continue in the currently uncertain economy as well, considering Apple’s strong balance sheet and the sizable share buybacks. Although Apple is far from a risk-free investment, its $115 plus billion in cash and marketable securities and close to $70 billion in stock buybacks over the past nine months should support its stock price and mitigate some risk for investors.
Unique Position In The Generative AI Space
Part of the current technology rally has been driven by excitement surrounding generative artificial intelligence. While Apple is a bit late to the party, with its new Apple Intelligence offering (which includes upgrades to its Siri voice assistant, new writing assistance tools, calculator features, and image generation), the company’s implementation of AI appears impressive. This is in contrast with many other big tech players who have been yet to find a solid use case or business model from generative AI. Now Apple has limited compatibility of the new software features to its top-end devices such as the iPhone 15 Pro and iPads with M-series processors, meaning that the vast majority of Apple consumers will need to upgrade devices to get access to AI capabilities. Moreover, unlike other big tech players who have set aside tens of billions of dollars on AI related capex outlays, Apple is likely to leverage more on-device processing.
AAPL stock has seen strong gains of 60% from levels of $130 in early January 2021 to around $210 now, vs. an increase of about 40% for the S&P 500 over this roughly 3-year period. However, the increase in AAPL stock has been far from consistent. Returns for the stock were 35% in 2021, -26% in 2022, and 49% in 2023. In comparison, Arista Networks, another company that also benefits from generative AI, has seen its stock surge by 300% over the same period. Arista is a market leader in high-speed networks catering to hyper-scalers and big corporations that are major stakeholders in the generative AI trend. Turns out, Arista is part of the 30-stock Trefis High Quality Portfolio, which has outperformed the S&P 500 each year over the same period. Why is that? As a group, HQ Portfolio stocks provided better returns with less risk versus the benchmark index; less of a roller-coaster ride as evident in HQ Portfolio performance metrics. Now, will Apple stock rally further going forward?
We think there is some upside for Apple, with our $219 price estimate for the stock coming in slightly ahead of the current market price. There are a couple of reasons for our positive stance on Apple. While continued revenue growth and solid margin expansion should drive Apple’s profits, shareholder returns could be magnified by Apple’s massive stock buyback program. Apple has bought back an average of about 5% of its stock each year over the last five years. Apple’s Valuation also appears reasonable, relative to historical levels. The stock trades at a P/E of about 28x currently, based on FY’25 consensus earnings. This is below the 31x the stock traded at in 2021 and 38x in 2020. This could make Apple reasonably compelling in the current market. title: Council Post: Understanding And Leveraging AI “Hallucinations” To Boost Innovation
text:
Perry Carpenter is Chief Human Risk Management Strategist for KnowBe4, developer of Security Awareness Training & Phishing Simulation tools.
The recent emergence of generative AI tools has captured the attention of businesses and the imagination of people everywhere. Readily accessible and often freely available, GenAI tools have fostered both awe and anxiety for many who recognize both the power and the potential perils.
Hallucinations Of The Virtual Kind
One area of concern for potential risk is hallucinations. AI hallucinations are instances where the tools generate content that is incorrect—completely fabricated from the digital ether yet clothed in conviction. Hallucinations occur when an AI system combines information in unexpected and sometimes bizarre ways. Not always so bizarre, though, is the fact that many unsuspecting users rely on the information generated and accept it as credible. Think of it kind of like when a really smart human is asked about something they don’t know, but instead of admitting they don’t know, they make up a very plausible (yet factually incorrect) answer.
Academics and scientists have called out GenAI tools, and there’s certainly plenty of evidence pointing to how these tools have innocently spread misinformation to the dismay of those using them.
For instance, two lawyers who unknowingly submitted mock case law completely fabricated by ChatGPT were fined $5,000 each by a federal judge. Even large tech companies can fall prey to these hallucinations. Google’s AI Overview feature went viral when users shared screenshots of the feature claiming they could use glue to stick cheese to pizza and recommending they eat one rock per day.
These and other perplexing examples point to the necessity of having a human in the loop when generating content or relying on information generated through these tools.
AI doesn’t have the ability to discern what’s real versus what’s plausible, which can lead to convincing, but potentially false, outputs. AI is trained on vast amounts of data stores and can recognize and replicate known patterns but cannot always (at least not yet) discern the context of patterns or their veracity. Consider the massive amount of false, intentional disinformation that’s available on the web exploited for political expediency to manipulate sentiments. When engineered to self-train, these large language models may collect both true and false narratives equally without making much distinction between the two.
Ultimately, AI’s goal is to create coherent and convincing content—even if that content isn’t accurate or factual. Fact-checking should become a habitual practice just to avoid embarrassing or costly missteps.
The Need For Human Intervention
By now it should be clear that GenAI outputs should not be blindly adopted or implemented without human intervention and oversight. To protect business interests and brand value, it's important to understand the limitations of these tools, including their propensity for hallucinations. To avoid these missteps, I recommend using AI outputs only as a starting point, not as the final authority on any topic, and establishing processes and policies to guide employee use of these tools. Always double-check facts (especially numbers) and information produced by GenAI; oversight by subject matter experts can help you ensure that any information used is accurate and credible. Also, be aware of potential biases that can creep into AI outputs based on the training data that has been used.
I believe that with an appropriate level of human oversight, organizations can actually benefit in unique ways from the propensity of AI tools to hallucinate. Hallucinations can represent an interesting starting point for creative insights and new ideas.
Drawing Creative Potential From Potential Peril
In the right context, hallucinations can be one of the main superpowers of generative AI, allowing these tools to generate images, write poems, help with blogs and become a brainstorming partner. It’s always a welcome surprise when GenAI coughs up novel content that has worth. The ability to produce unexpected combinations of ideas can be a valuable trait, something once exclusive to human creativity. Users can leverage AI’s ability to comb through massive amounts of data and information to help direct even bigger and better innovations.
Consider, for instance, some of the prompts professionals in various fields might use to help them brainstorm and generate unique ideas:
• Request “out of the box” solutions to vexing business problems.
• Ask the AI tool to “imagine” specific scenarios and make suggestions for how to address or leverage them.
• Find examples of past communication campaigns and requests for new approaches that may resonate with specific target audiences or demographics.
• Present a series of “what if” scenarios and prompt the tool for suggested solutions.
The key is that the responses to these prompts can provide inputs for team members to consider, enhance and expand upon to benefit from the random tendency of AI tools to hallucinate. After all, hallucinating—or making things up—is what drives brainstorming and the creative process. Imagining “what if” scenarios unhampered by the need to be rooted in reality can assist you in discovering potential solutions to intractable problems, creating “blue sky” scenarios or areas of exploration for product and service innovation.
AI hallucinations are a double-edged sword for businesses and brands. They can be damaging, as some notable examples illustrate. But they can also represent new ways to think differently about a wide range of topics and business challenges. Implementing strong governance and verification processes, as well as training users to proceed with caution, can help organizations benefit from the unique value these tools offer while avoiding unnecessary risk.

title: Council Post: Innovative Data Strategies: Leveraging AI For Smarter Enterprise Operations
text:
Bhaskar Gangipamula is the President and Co-Founder at Quadrant Technologies.
In the modern business world, where large volumes and complexities of corporate data are growing at an unprecedented rate, information is a challenge. And yet, at the same time, it is also an opportunity for service-based companies to draw insights. The density of information is growing exponentially, and artificial intelligence (AI) is a game-changer for how businesses manage, analyze, and get more value out of their data assets.
Here's how AI is reshaping enterprise data pipelines, from improving data quality to driving smarter decision-making.
The AI-Powered Evolution Of Data Management
The enterprise data platform was a labor-intensive process prone to errors and inefficiencies. AI is streamlining these processes through automation and intelligent algorithms fine-tuned with organization-specific business context.
AI-powered tools can:
1. Ensure strong data quality and ETL management: AI models can automatically identify and correct inconsistencies, handle code errors, and understand data architecture and upstream dependencies. Modern frameworks enrich data by adding context and relevant information from external sources. Multiagent frameworks build on that further by fixing pipelines, setting up alerts, suggesting code improvements, and solving the problem of congestion in enterprise data engineering. These frameworks guarantee strong and effective data quality and ETL management optimization across the entire data processing workflow.
2. Classify and categorize data: AI can go through unstructured data, such as textual documents or images, and classify them so they can be found, easily used, and customized with natural language questions.
3. Uncover hidden patterns: AI-driven data analytics can sift through massive amounts of data to identify patterns, trends and correlations that would be impossible for humans to detect. Additionally, AI can apply transfer learning, leveraging knowledge from one business system to another, to identify new relationships between data sets. This capability can help businesses uncover deeper insights and make the most of their data, leading to more informed and strategic decision-making.
4. Guide storytelling with data: Multi-agent frameworks, which are orchestrated and powered by AI, perform analysis like a symphony. Each agent specializes in a specific task, while humans in the loop work together on the extraction of meaningful insights from increasingly complex enterprise data landscapes. It's a smart pipeline—a transformation of raw information into actionable knowledge that empowers businesses to make confident decisions.
AI-Driven Decision-Making
AI is not only improving data management but also transforming how businesses make decisions. AI-powered analytics platforms can provide real-time insights, enabling organizations to react quickly to changing market conditions and customer needs.
Additionally, AI can help mitigate bias in decision-making by providing data-driven recommendations. AI decisions are backed by data and critical thinking, as the AI framework is built with consideration for a company's core business policies. This ensures the insights and recommendations align with the strategic objectives and operational standards of the organization.
Challenges And Considerations
While the benefits of AI in enterprise data solutions are undeniable, several challenges need to be addressed. Ensuring data privacy and security is paramount, especially as AI models often rely on sensitive information. The explainability of AI-generated insights is also crucial, as businesses need to understand the reasoning behind recommendations.
Additionally, companies tend to trust AI models that are guaranteed by their cloud providers, as the AI is hosted within their own cloud environment and data is not stored externally. This assurance is vital for maintaining control and compliance.
The Future Of AI In Enterprise Data
The future of AI in enterprise data solutions is incredibly promising. As AI technology continues to advance, I believe we can expect even more sophisticated tools and applications to emerge.
Recent research from MIT, particularly the development of GenSQL, highlights the potential of generative AI in databases. GenSQL utilizes probabilistic models for data transformations, making complex statistical analyses more accessible and accurate. This innovation exemplifies how AI can revolutionize data querying, anomaly detection, and synthetic data generation, paving the way for more powerful and user-friendly enterprise data solutions.
Final Thoughts
AI is revolutionizing the way we provide business services and manage data. By automating processes, uncovering insights, and enabling data-driven decision-making, AI is not only streamlining operations but also unlocking new opportunities for growth and competitiveness.
Embracing AI as a strategic tool is essential for organizations looking to thrive in the data-driven age, as it opens new doors for service-based companies to build AI-powered pipelines for better handling of data.

title: Council Post: How Small Businesses Can Use AI To Get A Competitive Edge
text:
Jason Leverant serves as the President and Chief Operating Officer of the AtWork Group, an award-winning national staffing firm.
Artificial intelligence (AI) is designed to analyze large amounts of data and use algorithms to complete tasks and automate business operations, which can help increase the productivity of its users. The use of this technology is spreading across numerous industries, including financial services, e-commerce and transportation, helping businesses improve training, enhance customer service, facilitate hiring and more.
But strategic deployment of AI isn’t just for the Fortune 500. Small businesses can also leverage free or low-cost AI tools to level the playing field in many areas.
Empowering Small Business
As AI technology continues to make strides, free online resources such as ChatGPT, Jasper AI and Google Gemini are making it easier for small businesses to harness the power of this new technology. For example, in a bid to increase AI’s availability to the masses, Apple debuted Apple Intelligence in June for iPhones, iPads and Macs. The new technology combines the power of generative AI models with personal context to help users manage email, enhance writing and improve images. Small businesses can turn to generative AI tools like these to help them improve productivity and strategic planning, and many are finding creative ways to use them successfully.
For example, businesses with fewer than 10 employees whose revenue increased over the past six months are more likely to have used AI, according to a survey conducted by GoDaddy. At least 44% of survey participants believe AI will help them compete with larger businesses. However, despite the potential for AI, 45% of small-business owners are not confident using AI, and understanding how to get started can be challenging.
How To Get Started
Small-business owners already have a long to-do list, and adding new technology to the mix can be daunting. However, I believe that AI can be a positive, cost-saving resource for your business, so it is well worth the effort to learn and take advantage of this resource. Based on the knowledge my staffing franchise has gained from testing various AI applications, here are a few benefits of implementing AI tools effectively.
1. Decrease costs.
Consider using AI to help your business stay on budget. AI can be used to automate administrative tasks and improve inventory management, as well as minimize the need to hire outside service providers to handle your marketing and expenses. By relying on AI for routine tasks, such as receipt tracking and transcribing meetings, you’ll have more time for strategic planning and improving efficiency. While AI won’t ever eliminate the need for a human touch, it can help you create a budget and analyze financial data to forecast trends.
2. Improve customer service.
Chatbots and automated response systems offer a 24/7 customer service solution that can help trim labor costs. You can also use AI to create customized interactions to provide personalized service. When you turn to chatbots and AI personalization, it’s important to remember they’re only one tool in your arsenal. AI technology improves each day, but you still need to make it easy for customers or clients to connect with a person. We’ve all tried to ask a chatbot a question but have not gotten the answer we need. You don’t want to let your customer service suffer when experimenting with new technology.
3. Automate recruitment.
Recruitment and retention are a top concern for small-business owners, according to Guidant Financial. At least 33% of small-business owners find the hiring process “somewhat” or “very difficult.” Consider using AI tools to help you write job descriptions and scan résumés to streamline hiring. AI tools can scan data from a variety of places, such as online job postings, social media networks and networking sites, to find qualified candidates.
Taking advantage of AI resources can also prevent any unconscious bias based on race, gender or age, promoting workplace diversity. Initially, there were some concerns about résumé bias when using AI technology for recruitment, and nearly half of employed job seekers believe AI tools are more biased than humans. If you use AI correctly, such as programming it to ignore demographic information, you can take steps to eliminate hiring bias. New programs such as Textio, which is designed to eliminate biased language in job posts, are making strides to improve AI-powered recruiting tools.
4. Enhance training.
Consider using AI to help you enhance your training program and improve employee retention. AI can customize training programs based on each employee’s proficiency level. Use its translation services to appeal to candidates who learn better in their first language. You can also create AI-simulated solutions and rely on virtual reality to facilitate an immersive training experience.
In addition to practical, everyday uses, AI is a great brainstorming tool that can help your business stay nimble and keep up with the competition. I am learning firsthand that when used effectively, AI can help small businesses achieve new heights.

text:

title: AI’s Role Human Trafficking And Digital Grooming
text:
In an era where technology advances at the speed of hyperchange (100 years of change in just 10 years), artificial intelligence (AI) has emerged as a powerful tool with vast potential. However, alongside its beneficial uses, AI, sadly, has also been exploited for nefarious purposes, including by human traffickers. This alarming trend involves traffickers using AI to identify, groom, and exploit potential victims, often without raising immediate suspicion. This disturbing intersection of AI and human trafficking is rapidly growing and underscores the urgent need for awareness and action.
The Dark Alliance of AI and Human Trafficking
Human traffickers have exploited the digital age, harnessing AI to enhance their illicit activities and augment their channels and actions to prey upon the innocent. Already, bad actors created AI algorithms that enable traffickers to sift through vast amounts of online data to identify vulnerable individuals who can be targeted for exploitation. This manipulation often occurs on social media, online forums, and chat rooms where potential victims, particularly young people, may unknowingly interact with AI agents or algorithms designed to groom and lure them into trafficking situations.
AI Identification of Vulnerable Targets
Victim identification and assessment is one of the primary ways traffickers use AI. By analyzing social media activity, predators exploit AI algorithms to target individuals who display signs of vulnerability, such as those going through emotional distress, financial hardship, or social isolation. Consequently, these bad actors become experts in grooming tactics for each target based on the AI recognizing patterns in online behavior and vulnerability assessment.
Grooming and Manipulation Through AI Chatbots
In the trafficker’s arsenal, AI powers yet another tool. These chatbots engage victims in seemingly genuine conversations and build trust over time. They are created to mimic human emotions and responses, making them highly effective in manipulating victims. The ultimate goal is to coerce the individual into a trafficking situation under false pretenses, such as promising a romantic relationship, a lucrative job opportunity, or a better life. In effect, predators use AI to generate leads for victims through social media and then use AI chatbots to close the deal.
Where Are the Real-World Examples and Case Studies
Sadly, direct public instances of AI specifically used for human trafficking are not widely documented, mainly due to the clandestine nature of these crimes. However, law enforcement does have numerous reports and studies showing the use of sophisticated AI technology by traffickers. For example, in online sex trafficking, perpetrators used AI tools for aggregating and analyzing data from various websites to identify potential victims and buyers. In some reported cases, traffickers used AI to optimize the scheduling and logistics of exploiting trafficking victims. In other words, law enforcement has seen predators leverage AI to facilitate their monetization and operations.
The Erosion of Digital Safety and Security
AI integration into human trafficking operations presents significant challenges and risks. The sophisticated nature of these AI tools makes it increasingly difficult for law enforcement and anti-trafficking organizations to detect and intervene in these activities. Additionally, the psychological impact on victims of AI enabled grooming and trafficking can be devastating, often leading to long-term trauma.
Furthermore, the misuse of AI for trafficking purposes raises serious concerns about digital safety and security, particularly for young and vulnerable internet users. It undermines the trust in digital platforms and highlights the need for robust safety measures to protect users from such exploitation. People live in a world where our digital footprint is rapidly expanding, with or without our consent. Unfortunately, minors have the most risk because they are engaging in platforms, chatbots, and so forth without knowledge of bad actors, let alone their intent.
Legal and Ethical Challenges
Many people ask why legal and judicial systems seem slow in combating these horrific issues. Regrettably, the use of AI in human trafficking presents complex legal and ethical challenges. Current laws and regulations do not adequately address the nuances of AI enabled crimes. Congruently, there's an ethical imperative for technology companies to ensure their platforms and AI technologies are not exploited for trafficking purposes. However, these companies have countered that they are not fully responsible for the content and intended use (or misuse) of what happens on the platform. In other words, there is a caveat emptor attitude that pushes back on users with the expectation that people understand the risks from bad actors.
As a result, legal frameworks need to be updated and strengthened to address, specifically, the use of AI in human trafficking. This involves not only penalizing traffickers who use AI for these purposes but also creating guidelines for responsible AI development and deployment. Moreover, this may need to include guidelines along institutional acquiesce, or even cover up support, in actions that protect these predators as a “side effect” of protecting the institution’s business interests.
Combating AI Powered Human Trafficking
Tackling the issue of AI powered human trafficking requires a comprehensive and multi-faceted approach. This includes enhancing legal frameworks, promoting ethical AI development, increasing public awareness, and fostering collaboration among various stakeholders. Moreover, as creators and developers of use cases and technology, we all have a role in the ethical development and use of AI to prevent its exploitation for trafficking. AI companies and developers must prioritize ethical considerations in their work, implementing safeguards to prevent the misuse of their technologies. This means thinking beyond the intended use and considering how bad actors could abuse and misuse the technology.
A critical first step is enhancing the detection and monitoring of AI trafficking activities. We can achieve this through the development of AI tools that identify signs of digital grooming and trafficking activities, coupled with human oversight to ensure accuracy and sensitivity. In effect, we can turn the table on how bad actors are abusing the technology.
A second step is raising public awareness and improving digital literacy about the risks of AI fueled human trafficking. Education campaigns can help inform the public, especially young internet users, about how to recognize and protect themselves from online grooming and exploitation.
The third step is improving collaboration and information sharing among tech companies, law enforcement, and anti-trafficking organizations are key. This includes sharing knowledge, best practices, and technological resources to stay ahead of traffickers. This step is vital to effectively combating AI trafficking.
In the end, AI use in human trafficking is a disturbing yet crucial issue that must be addressed. As the technology continues to evolve, so do the tactics of traffickers, making it imperative to stay vigilant and proactive in safeguarding vulnerable populations. By strengthening legal frameworks, promoting ethical AI development, enhancing detection, and monitoring capabilities, raising public awareness, and fostering stakeholder collaboration, we can make significant strides in combating this modern form of slavery. The fight against AI powered human trafficking is not just a technological challenge; it's a moral and social imperative that demands our collective effort and resolve.

title: AI And The Talent Development Revolution
text:
In history, few figures embody the spirit of continuous learning and adaptive leadership like Julius Caesar, a military pioneer of the Roman Empire. Caesar's strategic brilliance and relentless pursuit of knowledge set him apart as a leader who not only commanded armies but also understood the importance of evolving his tactics and strategies. His dedication to learning from every campaign, adapting to new circumstances, and leveraging the strengths of his diverse legions laid the groundwork for his unparalleled success. In today's rapidly changing world, the lessons from Caesar's leadership are more relevant than ever, especially as we integrate AI into the development of future leaders.
Embracing the AI Revolution in Leadership Development: As we stand on the brink of the fourth industrial revolution - integrating artificial intelligence (AI) into leadership and talent development - continuous learning represents an unprecedented opportunity. Tailored learning, real-time feedback, mentorship, and easily accessible tools for growth continue to be the core drivers of engagement and retention. Employee engagement has extremely tangible business and people outcomes — nothing new to report here. It has been shown to lead to an 81% reduction in absenteeism, a 10-25% increase in customer loyalty, and most importantly, a 23% increase in profitability. High engagement rates also signal that employees feel satisfied with and energized by their work experience and development opportunities.
Despite this, many employers still haven’t zeroed in on engagement as a business-critical priority. Gallup data still shows that only 33% of employees report feeling engaged, and our experience at EXCELR8 uncovered that only one in three HR leaders consistently track metrics like engagement and turnover.
AI is not just a tool for automation and efficiency; it is a transformative force that can reshape how leaders are nurtured and evolved. To thrive in this dynamic environment, organizations must harness the power of AI to foster agile, adaptive, and forward-thinking leaders.
Five Top Areas of AI-Driven Talent Development
1 - Personalized Learning and Development
AI enables highly personalized learning experiences, tailoring content to individual needs and learning styles. This approach ensures leaders receive the right training at the right time, maximizing their growth potential.
- Adaptive Learning Platforms: AI-driven platforms that adjust to the learner's pace and understanding, providing customized pathways.
- Behavioral Analytics: Tools that analyze learning patterns to recommend specific resources and activities.
- Skill Gap Analysis: AI identifies skill gaps and suggests targeted development opportunities to address them.
2 - Real-Time Feedback and Coaching
Instant feedback is crucial for continuous improvement. AI-powered tools can provide real-time insights, helping leaders refine their skills and strategies promptly.
- AI Mentors: Virtual coaches that offer immediate feedback and guidance based on performance data.
- Sentiment Analysis: Tools that assess communication and interaction, providing insights into emotional intelligence and engagement.
- Performance Metrics: Real-time tracking of key performance indicators, allowing for timely interventions and adjustments.
3 - Enhanced Decision-Making
AI can process vast amounts of data to support decision-making, helping leaders make informed and strategic choices.
- Predictive Analytics: Tools that forecast trends and outcomes based on historical data.
- Decision Support Systems: AI-driven systems that provide scenario analysis and risk assessment.
- Data Visualization: Advanced visualization techniques that make complex data comprehensible and actionable.
4 - Leadership Simulations and Virtual Reality (VR)
Immersive technologies like VR offer realistic simulations, enabling leaders to practice and refine their skills in a safe environment.
- Scenario-Based Training: VR simulations that replicate challenging leadership situations for practice.
- Soft Skills Development: Interactive modules focusing on communication, negotiation, and conflict resolution.
- Team Dynamics: Virtual environments where leaders can practice team-building and collaborative problem-solving.
5 - Continuous Learning Ecosystems
AI fosters ecosystems that promote lifelong learning, ensuring leaders remain adaptable and ahead of the curve.
- Learning Management Systems (LMS): AI-enhanced platforms that offer continuous learning opportunities and much better content.
- Content Curation: AI tools that aggregate and recommend relevant learning resources, content, and learning modules.
- Collaborative Learning: Platforms that facilitate peer-to-peer learning and knowledge sharing.
Leading into the Future with AI: The future of leadership and talent development is intrinsically linked with AI's capabilities. By embracing AI, organizations can cultivate leaders who are not only capable of navigating today's complexities but are also equipped to lead with vision and innovation into the future. Continuous learning, supported by AI, transforms leadership from a static set of skills into a dynamic, evolving journey. As we move forward, the integration of AI into leadership development will be the cornerstone of building resilient, forward-thinking organizations. And like any sound initiative, there must be a strategy and integration that support the company mission and culture.
In this new era, the leaders who will make a difference are those who are committed to learning, adapting, and harnessing the power of AI. The journey is continuous, the potential is boundless, and the future of leadership is brighter than ever.

title: Revolutionizing Retail: How Generative AI Is Shaping The Future Of Shopping
text:
AI styling is re-shaping the retail shopping experience in both B2B and B2C markets, one outfit combination at a time
The cross-industry integration of generative artificial intelligence is revolutionizing the way consumers shop. From personalized chatbots enhancing customer interactions to innovative idea generation for marketing campaigns, generative AI is transforming retail by disrupting it. The future of shopping is changing, not only through consumer experiences but also business practices.
AI styling is a newer retail use case for generative AI that offers both a business-to-business (B2B) and business-to-customer (B2C) application, transforming how retailers curate personalized fashion recommendations and engage with their customers. In essence, AI Styling refers to the use of AI algorithms to provide personalized fashion recommendations to customers in the retail industry.

Further, Fortune Business Insights predicts substantial growth for global AI in the retail market, forecasting a market size of $85.07 billion by 2032. These statistics underscore the impact AI can have on the retail landscape
To navigate ethical considerations surrounding AI use effectively, businesses must confront them directly

One might choose a B2C approach over B2B in order to directly engage with consumers, and offer personalized solutions, fostering strong brand loyalty. Conversely, B2B provides potential for larger contracts and scalable revenue opportunities, catering to industry-specific needs with specialized expertise. Brands like Aiuta AI Stylist offer both B2B and B2C services using AI solutions.
Step 2 - Maximize Market Impact: Leveraging Gen AI's Competitive Advantage

However, if you’re an entrepreneur looking to innovate in the Gen AI space, you may find success by developing AI styling as a standalone product. Data shows that the time to embrace generative artificial intelligence (AI) in retail strategy is now

Stitch Fix's Outfit Creation Model (OCM), trained on millions of curated outfits, is able to generate millions of new outfit combinations daily. If one’s goal is market differentiation, then Stitch Fix’s approach to AI integration, which has been in-house since its inception, might be more suitable. Developing proprietary AI styling creates the opportunity for full control and ownership over AI-generated data and seamless integration with existing systems.
Step 4: Balancing Input: Stylist Input, Customer Input, or Both
Businesses can decide to incorporate stylist input, customer input—or both—into their AI development process. For those aiming to create a sophisticated AI styling tool, leveraging both stylist expertise and customer insights, such as past purchases and trend preferences, may be advantageous. For customer engagement, one should consider conversion rates, subscription enrollments, and customer retention, while comparing AI-styled recommendations to non-AI interactions. In terms of tech performance, seek to test recommendation accuracy, gather customer satisfaction scores on the AI styling experience, and quantify time saved by customers compared to manual methods.
Step 6: Ensuring Excellence: Implementing Quality Assurance
To uphold quality standards in AI styling, it’s important to implement AI performance metrics. Additionally, continuous refinement of recommendation algorithms, enhancement of image recognition capabilities, and provision of user-friendly interfaces are essential practices.

To navigate ethical considerations surrounding AI use effectively, businesses must confront them directly. Establishing internal policies early on to govern the ethical use of AI, mitigating bias, and proactively communicating with customers about AI usage and potential biases are essential steps toward fostering transparency and trust.
By implementing these 7 steps, entrepreneurs can take proactive steps towards revolutionizing retail AI integration. Artificial intelligence will remain a powerful force for transforming retail, shaping the future of shopping, and driving innovation in the industry, making it critical for entrepreneurs to harness its potential.

title: Will Apple Change Its iPhone 16 Feature Price Decision?
text:
This story was updated on August 12th with new details about Apple Intelligence.
Apple is clear about the price of its Apple Intelligence AI features that will debut on the iPhone 16: they’re free. How long they’re free for, or if free comes with an asterisk, remains to be seen.
Neil Shah, partner at Counterpoint Research, told CNBC that Apple could charge between $10 and $20 monthly for Apple Intelligence, potentially as part of the Apple One subscription service.
“Software and services make it more lucrative for Apple to pass it on with the Apple One subscription model,” Shah explained.
AI is expensive to develop and maintain, while Shah correctly says that subscription revenue is far too lucrative for tech companies to pass up. Google already charges $19.99 monthly for access to its Google One AI Premium plan, which bundles Gemini Advanced with 2TB of cloud storage. U.K. subscribers also get free access to Nest Aware and Fitbit Premium.
ChatGPT has a premium tier and Samsung has repeatedly warned users that Galaxy AI will only be free until 2025. The infrastructure is there for these companies to charge for access to their most advanced software. Considering the billions already spent on building these language models and the ongoing cost to maintain them, money has to be recouped.
But the question for these companies is whether the current crop of AI tools are impressive enough to be locked behind a paywall? Looking at the current lineup of AI tools, across all major smartphone makers, I don’t think they are.
There isn’t a compelling case to pay extra for Writing Tools, Genmoji, audio transcription, web page summaries, or a smarter Siri. It’s the same with Galaxy AI and Gemini, which are useful and enhance the smartphone experience. I frequently ask Gemini for a helping hand and I am often impressed by generative image editing and call transcription.
But they are not worth adding another direct debit to my current stack. I am comfortable and experienced with non-AI-enabled smartphones enough to work through the FOMO.
This is why I don’t think Apple will change its decision on charging for Apple Intelligence any time soon, there isn’t a compelling case to do so. AI is the shiny new trend, but there are signs people are losing trust in the technology. Charging for previously free features could mean alienating people even further from the tech they were already souring on.
There’s also the game of chicken between Samsung, Google and Apple on AI tools. Whoever decides to put up the paywall first may may face a public backlash, which will inform the decisions of rival companies. These AI features are also quite similar, so why would iPhone users pay to transcribe their calls when Samsung users don’t have to?
Google has provided free AI tools via its Pixel Feature Drop program since 2019 and I don’t think that will change any time soon. Its paid tier of AI tech is for a very specific version of the Gemini language model that is more advanced. Or it will cost you extra if you want to save more Magic Editor cloud saves outside of the designed 10-per-month allowance.
But day-to-day AI-powered Pixel features have remained free. Above all else, skills like Call Screen and Photomoji may be AI-influenced but they’re ultimately just more smartphone features.
Where will the line be drawn between a regular feature upgrade in a new OS update, and what is paywalled because it’s ‘AI’? And how can that be done without alienating users who have already paid hundreds, or thousands, for top-end hardware? Alongside existing subscriptions they already have with that company.
Paywalled AI tools may make financial sense because it costs billions to build and maintain this technology, but the implementation of that plan is complex. There will need to be a lot of development work to make these tools worth paying extra for and then some persuasive arguments about why they shouldn’t be free.
There are several hurdles to leap before a paid AI feature set becomes a reality. for that reason Apple Intelligence, Galaxy AI and Google AI will likely stay mostly free for the foreseeable future.
August 12th update: Bloomberg’s Mark Gurman claims that Apple will make Apple Intelligence a key marketing point when the iPhone 16 launches. All iPhone 16 models will run the company’s AI toolset, which will also work on the iPhone 15 Pro versions. Apple spending its marketing budget on promoting AI isn’t a surprise considering its the buzzword of the year and rivals have made the exact same move.
Samsung lead with Galaxy AI when the Galaxy S24 launched this year. Google is also teasing that its AI features will play a huge role in the upcoming Pixel 9’s usability.
Samsung has built up some goodwill by rolling out Galaxy AI to older handsets, going as far back as the Galaxy S22. Bloomberg says that Apple will do the same by releasing AI tools to select handsets from 2023, but there’s no mention of older devices reciving the same treatment.
In fact, Bloomberg claims that at least 8GB of memory is needed to run Apple Intelligence, which rules out anything below the iPhone 15 Pro. That may change if less demanding features can be run on lower specification hardware. Samsung released select AI tools to phones that can run them, for example the Galaxy S21 series only got Circle to Search. The Galaxy S22 lineup got almost all AI tools save for Instant Slow Mo, which requires more onboard processing power. Apple could follow a similar route if Apple Intelligence proves to be popular.

title: Publicis Sapient CEO Lays Out The Path To AI Transformation
text:
It seems like all businesses today want to make the transformation to use more technology—like generative AI functions—to improve what they do. I talked to Nigel Vaz, CEO of tech transformation consultant Publicis Sapient, about the right way to shift gears in your business.
This conversation has been edited for length, continuity and clarity. It was excerpted in the Forbes CEO newsletter.
What is the biggest roadblock between a business making a tech transformation plan and actually doing that tech transformation?
Vaz: The first step is where you start. Even framing it as a tech transformation, in and of itself, is part of the challenge. So many businesses need to go under a much broader business transformation, where technology will play a very central role.
So many businesses started this journey from the place of an IT transformation. This is first and foremost a business transformation. It is transforming a business to be more digital, and technology has a huge role to play in that. But first and foremost, you’ve got to reimagine it: Not taking the existing, legacy business model, legacy processes, legacy approaches, and simply porting them onto new technology. I’m often reminded of the early days of the internet, where companies used to say, ‘We’re doing online orders.’ The order would spit out of a fax machine in the warehouse, and people would run with the fax, trying to gather stuff up. That’s just taking a legacy environment to a digital context.
With AI, pretty much the entirety of the C-suite has to break out of their silos, which is much harder to do than historical tech transformations. Where does the role between sales, marketing and customer service end when you are interacting with a company, asking questions about an order? You’re asking questions about what was marketed, you’re then asking questions about what you bought, and then you’re asking questions about an issue you have with that order. The silos that historically existed in terms of functional departments or divisions are breaking down, which I think also creates challenges for organizations: Where are you in this construct?
Finally, I think the most important thing is most executives may have understood this idea of being digital historically, but AI has made it so their customers and the CEO are learning about it at the same time. You’ve got this huge amount of pressure from customers wanting to interact in different ways, people in your organization wanting to test things, and the C-suite is really excited about this, but it needs capital investment in a macro economic environment that’s extraordinarily tough. You’ve got this really big dichotomy playing out, also financially, where you've got a real challenge in terms of how the world is.
How do you see businesses doing in the technology aspect of AI transformation—in terms of things like infrastructure support or accessible and clean data that can be utilized by AI systems?
There’s a lot of complexity. Let’s start with the first things first. Whenever people say we need an AI strategy, often my first question will be: Do you have a data strategy? Without good data, there is no good AI. You have to start with [thinking] about all the different data sets in your organization that you need to start to connect in order to start to train models that the AI will be based on. A lot of the work we’re helping companies do is: How do you actually establish those data foundations? How do you think about those data sets and ways that you can leverage them in order to start to train models?
Then you come to the next tier in the stack, which is the applications. How do you deploy applications that allow you to build intelligence across the organization? What we’re seeing is lots of people got really excited and ran off and did a whole bunch of proof-of-concepts. They were like, ‘I’m trying to test this specific problem. I built my own AI application interface, and I connected it to my own data set.’ So you have a lot of these ‘stovepipes.’ They might have given you some immediate benefits, so you had a proof of concept, but it didn’t allow you to scale it across the organization. And worse, it was against the fundamental premise of AI in the first place, because real value comes from connecting disparate sources of data, which otherwise would not be connected.
At that application tier, we’re helping companies build sandboxes so their people don’t go out into the real world and toss this information into public AI platforms, harness that for their own learning, and regurgitate that potentially to competitors. We’re building application tiers that say, rather than simply building all these AI stovepipes, you need a sandbox where you can experiment and try things out.
Then we’re help[ing] companies make choices on what kind of AI models [they] want to run in this application stack. Are you thinking about open-source models versus closed-source? Large language models versus small language models? If you’re solving a very specific customer service query, a small language model trained on a specific subset of data will perform better on a compute basis, cost you less money in the cloud, from a latency perspective, deliver better performance. You don’t necessarily need GPT 4.0 to scan your email and summarize.
What are the use cases that meaningfully will allow you to demonstrate value in the business, that allows the organization to see how that could scale across the organization? Imagine most companies as a super tanker. If you spin off a lot of speed boats and they’re performing a lot of tricks on the side of the supertanker, most people in the tanker say the speedboat has no relevance to me. Then if you try to turn the tanker in one go, there’s too much change and too much inertia. You take too long, and you don’t deliver value quick enough. You want the use cases to be big enough that they can demonstrate applicability to the rest of the organization, but small enough that you can deliver value in a period that doesn’t cause the organization and their inertia to kick in.
Ultimately, when you think about infrastructure, that middle application tier is essentially where you are making choices on cloud platforms and AI models and application stacks. Our belief is you have to do that within the context of creating organizational capability, as opposed to either outsourcing it or creating a lot of small proof of concepts within your organization.
It’s been about a year and a half since ChatGPT hit the news and got everyone excited about generative AI. Where would you say most companies are now in terms of coming up with strategy, figuring out good use cases and thoughtfully getting some applications of AI to make a difference in their business?
It depends very much on where they were before the last year and a half. While AI became interesting to the average person in November 2022, the reality is we’ve been using AI for clients for going on 10 years. We’ve been using machine learning models in financial services and risk and in credit. We’ve been moving to predictive AI models, which basically started to analyze existing data and make predictions on where you were. And then this last wave of generative AI. I feel like if you were already on that journey as an organization, right? You were probably somebody that was further ahead in being able to deploy actual scale AI.
Where organizations were starting from scratch, where they hadn’t really invested in AI at all, they’re in that first phase, which is connecting the data foundations and then building sandboxes, and potentially, in some cases, doing small proof of concepts. In many cases, where you had made an investment before the last year and a half, those organizations are starting to deploy real commercial-grade AI in the market to solve very specific business problems. As an example, we’re working with a pharmaceutical client where we’re doing medical and legal reviews—essentially reviewing all of the material that they put out to consumers about vaccines, safety information, about marketing—and using AI to essentially not only vet that for compliance by geography, but also, in some cases, generate content on the basis of compliant regulations. In different markets around the world, those regulations are super complex, and huge amounts of lawyers are poring over this information, and we’ve got machine learning models.
For companies more at the beginning phase of this journey, what should they expect in terms of what they have to do, how long it will take to do it, and how many expected and unexpected twists and turns they will encounter?
[There are] three fundamental buckets of considerations. First, what is it that you’re trying to do? Because the value of this is not from moving the same legacy to this new world. The reimagination of what you’re trying to do is important, because I’ve seen people say, ‘Let’s try and do the same thing we were doing faster or better.’ Why would you do that? This context allows you to do something fundamentally different or better.
The second bucket is in making the right technology choices and picking the right sets of partners. That’s important because you’re going to need some kind of Sherpa if you’re going to go on this trek up Everest. You don’t want to sort of say, ‘Hey, we’re going to figure this out ourselves.’ If you're going to do that, you need people in the organization who’ve had some experience doing it.
The third set, which historically has not been a consideration for companies in the context of tech projects, is what are the ethical considerations? Some businesses have to ask themselves: If I’m using a closed model and I don’t know what that model has been trained on, how do I know that the recommendations it’s making on these issues actually, you know, fits with my ethical considerations? Or how do I know that it’s not furthering bias which already exists in my data set? We’re working with a bank in the context of mortgages, and looking at which people were getting mortgages. If you simply train the AI on the basis of that data set, and the same people who always got mortgages, the AI is going to accelerate that even further.
You have to correct for bias in the data set and in the AI model. This requires things like ethics, bias, looking at IP protection. All of these—what I would consider regulatory or policy issues—are the third bucket.
What should companies be doing in terms of hiring people who know how to use AI, or training their existing employees in these skills? When should they be doing that?
You can’t start soon enough. I would say yesterday is when you should have started. The rate of change, and the scale of change that is in front of us is exponential. If you look at ChatGPT, when it came out in November [2022], it might have been like a four-year-old child. And then you look at [version] 3.5, and it was like a 12-year-old. Then you look at, you know, kind of where [GPT-]4o is, and you look at where [OpenAI video generator] Sora is.
Much of what this journey is going to require is a commitment to learning, unlearning and relearning. You’re constantly going to learn new things. Then you’re going to have to unlearn them, because things have changed again, and you're going to have to relearn new things. You’re going to constantly be committed to this idea of becoming a learning organization in the way that you do things.
We’re seeing it at all levels. We did some experiments internally where we took software developers straight out of university and taught them how to work with AI the very first day that they started with the organization. And then we were looking at more seasoned developers who’ve been around for a while, who wrote much better code on a standalone basis, but may not necessarily have adopted these tools and ways of working. We started to measure the outputs of both of those groups, and what you realize is that change is not just for people who are entering the workforce. The biggest part of that change is for people who are in the workforce, and now need to do something fundamentally different.
Where do you see things with businesses developing and adopting AI applications in five years?
Five years will, I think, see the rise of intelligent organizations that can harness all the potential knowledge that is in the organization and in peoples’ heads, start[ing] to become organizations that can respond to and iterate on truly understand[ing] the context of all of the knowledge within the organization, act[ing] in real time on the basis of what it's learning about itself.
For example, if you are a CPG company and you have an issue with your supply chain in Russia or Ukraine, are you able to dynamically, in real-time, influence your marketing to not promote products that depend on that particular ingredient? Or are you able to swap out that ingredient for something else and reflect that in pricing? Those are the kinds of dynamic scenarios I think we’ll start to see, where human intervention historically was needed in huge amounts in order to start to make some of those decisions. There’s always going to be a need for people in the organization, but I think what those people do is going to be very different.
Is there anything else you wanted to add?
It’s a fascinating time. I feel a little bit like where we were in the late ‘90s, early 2000s with the internet. You knew this was going to be a fundamentally game-changing moment, yet at the same time, the hype cycle and the dot-com bubble was bursting, and I think a lot of people were questioning whether the internet was really going to be as big and as transformational as it was. I think the reason for that is they confused a silly website that attempted to do quick commerce or food delivery 25 years too soon with whether Marriott was going to be selling hotel rooms on the internet or not, or whether Walmart was going to be selling groceries online.
This is the same situation with AI. You get a lot of examples of things that are frivolous, but there’s other things that are going to profoundly shape the very nature of everything that we do in an organization, and with customers and with employees. I feel like that distinction is super important to recognize the potential of what’s coming.

title: How HUMAN Security Is Protecting The Digital Journey
text:
Digital interactions underpin nearly every facet of commerce, which makes it all the more concerning that the threats facing businesses and consumers continue to evolve in both scale and sophistication. Amid this growing complexity, HUMAN Security has emerged as a defender against cyber threats with a unique perspective on safeguarding the entire digital commerce journey.
I spoke with Sandy Carielli, principal analyst at Forrester and author of The Forrester Wave: Bot Management Software, Q3 2024 report, about the challenges organizations face. She explained, “What organizations are dealing with is just the influx of automation that is attempting to impersonate human traffic for purposes of fraud. That can be large numbers of login requests that are attempting to do credential stuffing. It can include attempts to do inventory hoarding, for example, hoarding Taylor Swift tickets is something I've seen.”
A Unique Perspective on Digital Defense
HUMAN Security's approach to cybersecurity is built on the understanding that the journey of digital commerce is intricate, involving multiple touchpoints where threats can emerge. As CEO Stu Solomon explained, "From the time that digital ad content is first bid on, then published, to when a consumer interacts with it, and finally makes decisions around account scenarios—we’re looking at fraud, risk decision-making at every step of that journey across the entire digital supply chain."
Solomon, who describes himself as a "data guy by trade," was drawn to HUMAN for this very reason. "We’re sitting on some of the most unique and scaled data you can imagine, seeing all of those transactions every single step of the way," he noted.
This holistic view is what differentiates HUMAN Security. By focusing on the entire lifecycle of digital interactions, the company offers a level of visibility and protection that few others can match.
Addressing the Modern Threat Landscape
One of the most pressing challenges in today’s cybersecurity landscape is the rise of bot networks and their use in manipulating elections and spreading disinformation. I was a contributing author to the book “Botnets,” which was published in 2007. In the past 17 years, a lot has changed—and yet surprisingly a lot hasn’t.
Carielli stressed, “One of the challenges we have is that the bots and the bot operators have just gotten so much smarter. So this is not a situation where you can install any sort of solution or protection that is static. It's a very ongoing, continuous, dynamic problem.”
According to Solomon, the threat posed by these bot networks is twofold: "They can create an inability at scale to provide connectivity to digital content—an age-old bot herding scenario. But more importantly, they allow for the amplification of disinformation, especially when combined with generative AI."
HUMAN Security is at the forefront of combating these threats. By using AI and machine learning to process vast amounts of data, HUMAN can quickly identify and neutralize bot-driven activities. This perspective is crucial, especially in the context of the company’s most recent update to the HUMAN Defense Platform, which now offers AI-derived capabilities like adaptive detection as threat actors pivot their tactics, malicious traffic attack profiling, and more.
Solomon emphasized the unique outcome that the AI is creating for HUMAN—and more importantly for its clients. The enhanced AI capabilities allow even less mature cybersecurity programs to quickly discern and take action on vast amounts of information, driving better mitigation strategies.
The Quadrillion Report: A Snapshot of Cyber Threats in the Last Year
HUMAN’s Quadrillion Report, released in July 2024, offers a comprehensive look at the current state of cyber threats, based on data from over one quadrillion digital interactions observed in 2023. Among the report’s most striking findings is the rise of AI-powered attacks, particularly those targeting account credentials.
As Solomon explained, "AI allows attackers to crack credentials by feeding large language models a username or email address and then predicting what a new password might be based on patterns in old ones."
Despite the increasing sophistication of these attacks, HUMAN's AI capabilities continue to detect and thwart them effectively, according to Solomon. The report also highlights the ongoing mistrust of LLMs among HUMAN’s customers, with 80% opting to block them outright.
However, the same AI tools that empower attackers also empower defenders. Solomon stressed, "Defenders are becoming more effective, and are starting to close the gap that we've been trying to close for years around the dynamic nature of the adversary moving faster than the pace of defense."
Looking Ahead: The Future of Cybersecurity
As cyber threats continue to evolve, so too does HUMAN Security’s approach to defending against them. Solomon sees the future of cybersecurity as one that is increasingly intertwined with AI and data integrity. "AI security boils down to data integrity—do you trust what goes in, do you trust what comes out, and is it being used in the way that it's intended to?" he asks. This emphasis on trust and integrity is at the core of HUMAN’s mission, ensuring that the digital commerce journey remains secure from start to finish.
By protecting brands across the entire digital commerce journey and leveraging AI in innovative ways, HUMAN is not just responding to threats—they’re striving to stay ahead of them. As Solomon succinctly puts it, "We’re on a convergence path, predicated on the age-old understanding that to protect the future, we must first secure the present."

title: How Google’s Pixel 9 Pro Will Change Smartphones Forever
text:
Updated August 12 with details on three leaked features and their potential roll-out across Android; and details on the competing iPhone 16 AI software.
Next week will see the launch of the Pixel 9 family of smartphones at the titular Made By Google event. The annual event allows Google to demonstrate what it believes a smartphone should represent. Last year’s Pixel 8 family offered new displays, improved cameras, updated software and its custom-designed Tensor Mobile chipset.
All of those changes allowed Google to pitch the Pixel 8 and Pixel 8 Pro as the AI-first smartphones. In the process it defined how generative AI would be introduced to the mobile world. One year later, with that view of the market now the norm, Google can build on that success, entrench its view of smartphone AI, and control the vital high ground of artificial intelligence.
This week, Google gets to do it all again except this time, it’s not about defining the market but fortifying it.
Google has several AI tools the Pixel platform has demonstrated, and similar tools are available from several Android manufactuers. You have tools to remove, move, or edit individual elements of a photo; you have the option to move expressions between photos to get the best composite image possible, and you have tools to clean up audio recorded in a video.
You have tools for transcribing audio, summarising information from web pages and emails, and searching based on a screenshot or even a circled part of the screen. AI can help screen spam calls, act as a translator while travelling, and suggest replies, topics, and more when creating on your phone.
All of these debuted on the Pixel 8 family before echoing throughout the ecosystem. In fact, Google’s circle to search feature actually debuted with Samsung’s Galaxy AI platform, which mirrored many of the Pixel features and added in many of its own. Other manufacturers introduced their own AI tools, and chip manufacturers ensured support for AI routines were hardwired to support AI code.
These all followed the same direction and ethos Google laid down in public with the Pixel 8. That direction will only be emphasised this week with the launch of the Pixel 9 and a raft of new AI features.
Update: Monday August 12: As well as the potential rebranding of the suite to “Google AI”, the team at Lifehacker have picked out three potential AI tools that could be debuting at tomorrow’s "Made By Google" event:
"These features include Add Me, a feature that might use AI to add extra people to a photo; Studio, which appears to be an AI image generator; and Pixel Screenshots, which may scan the screenshots in your library, turning them into an easy-to-search database."
They also note that these features are expected to need the presumptively named Tensor Mobile G4 chipset, which will make its debut across the Pixel 9 range. Apple is taking a similar approach when the iPhone 16 platform launched, limiting its Apple Intelligence suite to either the brand-new handsets or last year’s premium-priced iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max.
It’s not unknown for Android manufacturers to release their AI services for a new handset or chipset before rolling them back through the portfolio; Samsung’s Galaxy AI was launched for the Galaxy S24 family in January, and naturally, as a keystone of the Z Fold6 and Z Flip6 launches last week. Yet Samsung has ported these back to older Galaxy S models and is working on bringing as many of the features as possible to the Galaxy A35 and A55 handsets.
While the new features may help sell the Pixel 9 family, ultimately, they should become available across the full Android platform, solidifying Google’s vision of AI smartphones.
There’s also another competitive aspect with the rise of genre-defining AI in Android. Apple is nowhere to be seen.
Update: Sunday August 11: How much of a challenge will Apple’s iPhone offer in the battle to define generative AI for the 2024/25 season of smartphone releases? Two key factors will be the uptake of the new handsets and the availability of the software.
Gurman, as well as confirming the four iPhone models that will be revealed in September (namely the iPhone 16, iPhone 16 Plus, iPhone 16 Pro, and iPhone 16 Pro Max), also looks at the potential for an increase in sales and a larger than usual uptake of new handsets. This is an important point for those measuring the impact of the awkwardly backronymed Apple intelligence suite; apart from last year’s top-tier iPhone 15 Pro and iPhone 15 Pro Max, Apple will not backport its generative AI tools to countless existing users.
Effectively no new hardware means no adoption of Apple Intelligence. According to the latest financial projections offered to investors by Apple, the company is not planning or expecting any significant boost in sales. There will be new handsets, but don’t expect a sudden rush of upgrades to increase the user base for Apple’s AI plans.
Without a wave of existing iPhone users to capture the zeitgeist, Apple will struggle to change the discussions around generative AI on smartphones away from that decided by Google and its Android partners.
Google’s Pixel launch happened two weeks after the iPhone 15 and iPhone 15 Pro were released. Apple’s September launch did not feature generative AI or any of the new frontiers about to be explored. Arguably, the iPhone 15 family was the last of the great smartphone pillars to launch without AI. Apple’s first chance to talk about AI for the iPhone did not arrive until its Worldwide Developer Conference in June.
The awkwardly backronymed Apple Intelligence software would not be available immediately; it would have to wait for September’s launch of the iPhone 16 family. It would not be backported to any existing iPhone (except for 2023’s iPhone 15 Pro and 15 Pro Max). Neither will Apple Intelligence be ready for the September 2024 launch of the iPhone 16. A limited set of tools will be included in an October update to iOS, a basic ChatGPT implementation by the end of the year, and the full package displayed at WWDC will only arrive in the first half of 2025.
Apple has still to catch up with the first generation of AI smartphones,
Meanwhile, Google is pushing Android forward with the second generation of AI smartphones ready to be revealed to the public. Google is the company that will make the decision on the future direction of AI.
